documentNotes.title: Please read this first:
documentNotes.statement:
1. The time available is 5 hours for the theoretical competition.
2. Use only the pen provided.
3. Use only the front side of the paper.
4. Begin each part of the problem on a separate sheet.
5. For each question, in addition to the ***blank sheets*** where you may write, there is an ***answer form*** where you *must* summarize the results you have obtained. Numerical results should be written with as many digits as are appropriate to the given data.
6. Write on the blank sheets of paper whatever you consider is required for the solution of the question. Please use *as little text as possible*; express yourself primarily in equations, numbers, figures, and plots.
7. Fill in the boxes at the top of each sheet of paper used by writing your ***Country No*** and ***Country Code,*** your student number (***Student No***), the number of the question ***(Question No)***, the progressive number of each sheet ***(Page No),*** and the total number of blank sheets used for each question ***(Total No of pages).*** Write the question number and the section letter of the part you are answering at the top of each sheet. If you use some blank sheets of paper for notes that you do not wish to be marked, put a large X across the entire sheet and do not include it in your numbering.
8. At the end of the exam, arrange all sheets for each problem *in the following order;*
   - answer form
   - used sheets in order
   - the sheets you do not wish to be marked
   - unused sheets and the printed question

   Place the papers inside the envelope and leave everything on your desk. You are not allowed to take *any* sheets of paper out of the room.

transcription.notes: Problems document: clean text layer, used only as a spelling cross-check. Solutions document: text layer is garbled (custom font encoding), not usable. Pages 6–9 of the problems document are blank answer forms (header table and empty answer boxes for 1A, 1B, 1C, 1D, 2a, 2b, 3a–3d); they are not transcribed. Question 1 has four printed titled divisions 1a)–1d), transcribed as sections; the answer form labels them 1A–1D. Points per section add to 2.5 each; the paper prints no total (10 per question, 30 overall by sum). Kept as printed: “Avagadro’s number” (name misspelling, a name is never changed), “Stephan-Boltzmann” in the solution (name), “What should you vary( R and/or SG )” spacing, “[3pts]”, the solution’s “Gravitational force / Centrifugal force α m²r” where α stands for proportionality, “V_i′ − V_f with the correct polarity” in the 1c solution (the prime is printed), and the multiplication sign written as x in the vector products and numbers of the Question 3 solution. In the question statements the printed “x” in numbers such as 1.0x10-9 is rendered as ×10^{-9} in LaTeX. Solution of Question 3 does not follow the printed labels: Part 3a answers a) and b), Part 3b answers c), Part 3c answers d); Part 3c items 2 and 3 (phase π/36, skin depth, “The correct choice is (iii)”) belong to a different version of the question and are transcribed as printed. The printed point breakdown of Part 3a (4.0 pts) and Part 3c (item 1: 2.0 pts; items 2–3 extra) does not match the question’s printed points (a+b = 5.0, d = 3.0). The official 1b ratio is printed as 12. In 2b the solution uses m for the current mass of the ordinary star.

sections.title: 1a) KLYSTRON
sections.statement:
Klystrons are devices used for amplifying very high-frequency signals. A klystron basically consists of two identical pairs of parallel plates (cavities) separated by a distance $b$, as shown in the figure.

An electron beam with an initial speed $v_0$ traverses the entire system, passing through small holes in the plates. The high-frequency voltage to be amplified is applied to both pairs of plates with a certain phase difference (where period T corresponds to $2\pi$ phase) between them, producing horizontal, alternating electric fields in the cavities. The electrons entering the input cavity when the electric field is to the right are retarded and vice versa, so that the emerging electrons form bunches at a certain distance. If the output cavity is placed at the bunching point, the electric field in this cavity will absorb power from the beam provided that its phase is appropriately chosen. Let the voltage signal be a square wave with period $T=1.0\times10^{-9}$ s, changing between $V=\pm0.5$ volts. The initial velocity of the electrons is $v_0=2.0\times10^{6}$ m/s and the charge to mass ratio is $e/m=1.76\times10^{11}$ C/kg. The distance $\alpha$ is so small that the transit time in the cavities can be neglected. Keeping 4 significant figures, calculate;

figures.alt: Klystron schematic: an electron beam with velocity v0 (arrow) passes along a dotted line through two pairs of vertical plates. The input cavity plates (left pair, gap α) and output cavity plates (right pair, gap α) are separated by distance b. The input cavity is connected to an AC source (~) and, through a box labelled phase shifter, to the output cavity. Callout labels: input cavity, output cavity, phase shifter.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: the distance $b$, where the electrons bunch. Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[1.5 pts]*

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: the necessary phase difference to be provided by the phase shifter. Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[1.0 pts]*

sections.title: 1b) INTERMOLECULAR DISTANCE
sections.statement:
Let $d_L$ and $d_V$ represent the average distances between molecules of water in the liquid phase and in the vapor phase, respectively. Assume that both phases are at 100 °C and atmospheric pressure, and the vapor behaves like an ideal gas. Using the following data, calculate the ratio $d_V/d_L$ and copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[2.5 pts]*

Density of water in liquid phase: $\rho_L=1.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$,

Molar mass of water: $M=1.8\times10^{-2}$ kg/mol

Atmospheric pressure: $P_a=1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$

Gas constant: $R=8.3$ J/mol$\cdot$K

Avagadro’s number: $N_A=6.0\times10^{23}$ /mol

sections.title: 1c) SIMPLE SAWTOOTH SIGNAL GENERATOR
sections.statement: A sawtooth voltage waveform $V_0$ can be obtained across the capacitor $C$ in Fig. 1. $R$ is a variable resistor, $V_i$ is an ideal battery, and $SG$ is a spark gap consisting of two electrodes with an adjustable distance between them. When the voltage across the electrodes exceeds the firing voltage $V_f$, the air between the electrodes breaks down, hence the gap becomes a short circuit and remains so until the voltage across the gap becomes very small.

figures.caption: Figure 1
figures.alt: Circuit: ideal battery Vi (+ on top, − below) in series with a switch and a variable resistor R; the resistor feeds a node from which a spark gap SG and a capacitor C are connected in parallel to the lower rail; the output voltage V0 is taken across the capacitor between the + and − terminals on the right, shown with a double-headed arrow.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Draw the voltage waveform $V_0$ versus time $t$, after the switch is closed. *[0.5 pts]*

answer.note: Official solution: a sketch of repeated exponential charging of V0 towards Vi, cut off at Vf with period T.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: What condition must be satisfied in order to have an almost linearly varying sawtooth voltage waveform $V_0$? Copy your result onto the **answer form**. *[0.2 pts]*

parts.label: c)
parts.statement: Provided that this condition is satisfied, derive a simplified expression for the period $T$ of the waveform. Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[0.4 pts]*

parts.label: d)
parts.statement: What should you vary( $R$ and/or $SG$ ) to change the period only? Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[0.2 pts]*

parts.label: e)
parts.statement: What should you vary ( $R$ and/or $SG$ ) to change the amplitude only? Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[0.2 pts]*

parts.label: f)
parts.statement: You are given an additional, adjustable DC voltage supply. Design and draw a new circuit indicating the terminals where you would obtain the voltage waveform $V_0'$ described in Fig. 2. *[1.0 pts]*

figures.caption: Figure 2
figures.alt: Graph of V0′ versus t: a sawtooth that jumps up to the level Vf (dotted horizontal line) and falls linearly to zero, repeated three times.

answer.note: Official solution: a circuit with an additional supply (Vi − Vf) in series, with the correct polarity; V0′ is taken between the free terminal of this supply and the spark-gap node.

sections.title: 1d) ATOMIC BEAM
sections.statement: An atomic beam is prepared by heating a collection of atoms to a temperature $T$ and allowing them to emerge horizontally through a small hole (of atomic dimensions) of diameter $D$ in one side of the oven. Estimate the diameter of the beam after it has traveled a horizontal length $L$ along its path. The mass of an atom is $M$. Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[2.5 pts]*

figures.alt: A cubic oven filled with small spheres (atoms); a small hole on its right face emits a dotted horizontal beam. Labels: Diameter = D (at the hole), a double arrow L along the beam, Oven at temperature T, Atoms of mass M.

answer.note: Final result of 1d. 1a: b = 2.272×10⁻² m, Δφ = ±220° or ±140°; 1b: d_V/d_L = 12; 1c: V_i ≫ V_f, T = (V_f/V_i)RC, vary R (period), SG and R (amplitude).

sections.title: Part 1a
sections.statement:
a.

$$v_{ret}=\sqrt{v_0^2-2(e/m)V}=1.956\times10^{6}\ m/s$$

$$v_{acc}=\sqrt{v_0^2+2(e/m)V}=2.044\times10^{6}\ m/s$$

(0.5 pts)

sections.title: Part 1d
sections.statement:
As the beam passes through a hole of diameter D the resulting uncertainty in the y-component of the momentum;

$$\Delta p_y\approx\frac{\hbar}{D}$$

(0.6 pts)

and the corresponding velocity component;

$$\Delta v_y\approx\frac{\hbar}{MD}$$

(0.4 pts)

Diameter of the beam grows larger than the diameter of the hole by an amount

$\Delta D=\Delta v_y.t$ ,

where t is the time of travel. (0.2 pts)

If the oven temperature is T, a typical atom leaves the hole with kinetic energy

$$KE=\frac{1}{2}Mv^2=\frac{3}{2}kT$$

(0.4 pts)

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{3kT}{M}}$$

(0.2 pts)

Beam travels the horizontal distance L at speed v in time

$t=\dfrac{L}{v}$, so (0.2 pts)

$$\Delta D=t\Delta v_y\approx\frac{L}{v}\frac{\hbar}{MD}=\frac{L\hbar}{MD\sqrt{\frac{3kT}{M}}}=\frac{L\hbar}{D\sqrt{3MkT}}$$

(0.4 pts)

Hence the new diameter after a distance L will be;

$$D_{new}=D+\frac{L\hbar}{D\sqrt{3MkT}}$$

(0.1 pts)

parts.label: a)
parts.statement:
It is well known that most stars form binary systems. One type of binary system consists of an ordinary star with mass $m_0$ and radius $R$, and a more massive, compact neutron star with mass $M$, rotating around each other. In all the following ignore the motion of the earth. Observations of such a binary system reveal the following information:

- The maximum angular displacement of the ordinary star is $\Delta\theta$, whereas that of the neutron star is $\Delta\phi$ (see Fig. 1).
- The time it takes for these maximum displacements is $\tau$.
- The radiation characteristics of the ordinary star indicate that its surface temperature is $T$ and the radiated energy incident on a unit area on earth’s surface per unit time is $P$.
- The calcium line in this radiation differs from its normal wavelength $\lambda_0$ by an amount $\Delta\lambda$, due only to the gravitational field of the ordinary star. (For this calculation the photon can be considered to have an effective mass of $h/c\lambda$.)

Find an expression for the distance $\ell$ from earth to this system, only in terms of the observed quantities and universal constants. Copy your result onto the **answer form**. *[7 pts]*

figures.caption: Fig. 1
figures.alt: Two extreme positions of the binary seen from a telescope at distance ℓ: the ordinary star (large dot) at positions I and II and the neutron star (small dot) at positions II and I on a dashed line; dashed lines from each position converge on the telescope; the angle between the neutron-star lines is marked Δφ and between the ordinary-star lines Δθ. Legend: Ordinary star, Neutron star, Telescope.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Assume that $M\gg m_0$, so that the ordinary star is basically rotating around the neutron star in a circular orbit of radius $r_0$. Assume that the ordinary star starts emitting gas toward the neutron star with a speed $v_0$, relative to the ordinary star (see Fig. 2). Assuming that the neutron star is the dominant gravitational force in this problem and neglecting the orbital changes of the ordinary star find the distance of closest approach $r_f$ shown in Fig. 2. Copy your result onto the **answer form**. *[3pts]*

figures.caption: Fig. 2
figures.alt: The ordinary star m0 at the top emits a gas element (dm) moving with speed v0 downward; the gas follows a dashed elliptical path around the neutron star M at the bottom, approaching it to distance rf; the vertical separation between m0 and M is marked r0.

sections.title: Part 2a
sections.statement:
The total energy radiated per second = $4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$, where $\sigma$ is the Stephan-Boltzmann constant. The energy incident on a unit area on earth per second is;

$$P=\frac{4\pi R^2\sigma T^4}{4\pi\ell^2}\ \text{ yielding, }\ R=\left(P/\sigma T^4\right)^{1/2}\ell\quad(1)$$

(0.8 pts)

The energy of a photon is $hf=hc/\lambda$. The equivalent mass of a photon is $h/c\lambda$. Conservation of photon energy:

$$\frac{hc}{\lambda_0}-\frac{Gm_0}{R}\cdot\frac{h}{c\lambda_0}=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$$

(0.8 pts)

yielding

$$R=\frac{Gm_0(\lambda_0+\Delta\lambda)}{c^2\Delta\lambda}\quad(2)$$

and (2) yields,

$$m_0=\frac{c^2\Delta\lambda\left(P/\sigma T^4\right)^{1/2}}{G(\lambda_0+\Delta\lambda)}\ell\quad(3)$$

(0.2 pts)

The stars are rotating around the center of mass with equal angular speeds:

$\omega=(2\pi/2\tau)=\pi/\tau$ (4) (0.2 pts)

The equilibrium conditions for the stars are;

$$\frac{GMm_0}{(r_1+r_2)^2}=m_0r_1\omega^2=Mr_2\omega^2\quad(5)$$

(0.8 pts)

with

$$r_1=\ell\frac{\Delta\theta}{2},\ r_2=\ell\frac{\Delta\phi}{2}\quad(6)$$

(0.4 pts)

Substituting (3), (4) and (6) into (5) yields

$$\ell=\left(\frac{8c^2\Delta\lambda\left(P/\sigma T^4\right)^{1/2}}{\Delta\phi(\pi/\tau)^2(\lambda_0+\Delta\lambda)(\Delta\theta+\Delta\phi)^2}\right)^{1/2}.$$

(0.8 pts)

sections.title: Part 2b
sections.statement:
Conservation of angular momentum for the ordinary star;

$$mr^2\omega=m_0r_0^2\omega_0\quad(7)$$

(0.6 pts.)

Conservation of angular momentum for dm:

$$r^2\omega\,dm=r_f^2\omega_f\ dm\quad(8)$$

(0.6 pts)

where $\omega_f$ is the angular velocity of the ring. Equilibrium in the original state yields,

$$\omega_0=\left(\frac{GM}{r_0^3}\right)^{1/2}\quad(9)$$

(0.8 pts)

and (7), (8) and (9) give,

$$\omega=\frac{m_0r_0}{mr^2}\left(\frac{GM}{r_0}\right)^{1/2},\ \omega_f=\frac{m_0r_0}{mr_f^2}\left(\frac{GM}{r_0}\right)^{1/2}\quad(10)$$

(0.4 pts)

Conservation of energy for dm;

$$\frac{1}{2}dm\left(v_0^2+r^2\omega^2\right)-\frac{GM\ \mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{1}{2}dm\,r_f{}^2\omega_f{}^2-\frac{GM\ \mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{r_f}}\quad(11)$$

(1.2 pts)

Substituting (10);

$$v_0^2+\frac{m_0^2r_0GM}{m^2}\left(\frac{1}{r^2}-\frac{1}{r_f^2}\right)-2GM\left(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{r_f}\right)=0\quad(12)$$

Since $r_0\gg r_f$, if $r>r_0$, $r^{-1}$ and $r^{-2}$ terms can be neglected. Hence,

$$r_f=\frac{GM}{v_0^2}\left(\left(1+\frac{m_0^2r_0v_0^2}{GMm^2}\right)^{1/2}-1\right).$$

(0.8 pts)

To show that $r>r_0$ change in the linear momentum of the ordinary star in its reference frame:

$$-\frac{GMm}{r^2}+mr\omega^2-m\frac{dv_r}{dt}=-v_0\frac{dm_{gas}}{dt}\quad(13)$$

(0.8 pts)

and (13) implies the existence of an outward force initially and hence r starts growing. Using (7) one can write

$$mr\omega^2=\frac{m_0^2r_0^4\omega_0^2}{mr^3}\ .$$

Hence, $\dfrac{Gravitational\ force}{Centrifugal\ force}\,\alpha\ \mathrm{m}^2r$ . (0.4 pts)

where m is definitely decreasing. If r starts decreasing at some time also, this ratio starts decreasing, which is a contradiction.

So $r>r_0$. (0.4 pts)

problems.title: Question 3 — MAGNETOHYDRODYNAMIC (MHD) GENERATOR
problems.statement:
A horizontal rectangular plastic pipe of width $w$ and height $h$, which closes upon itself, is filled with mercury of resistivity $\rho$. An overpressure $P$ is produced by a turbine which drives this fluid with a constant speed $v_0$. The two opposite vertical walls of a section of the pipe with length $L$ are made of copper.

The motion of a real fluid is very complex. To simplify the situation we assume the following:

- Although the fluid is viscous, its speed is uniform over the entire cross section.
- The speed of the fluid is always proportional to the net external force acting upon it.
- The fluid is incompressible.

These walls are electrically shorted externally and a uniform, magnetic field **B** is applied vertically upward only in this section. The set up is illustrated in the figure above, with the unit vectors $\hat{x}$, $\hat{y}$, $\hat{z}$ to be used in the solution.

figures.alt: Perspective drawing of a horizontal rectangular pipe section of width w and height h with fluid velocity v (hatched arrow) flowing to the right; a length L of the pipe has copper side walls (dotted shading) joined by shorting wires over the top (labelled Shorting wires); vertical arrows B pass upward through the section; curved hatched arrows at both ends indicate the closed circulation; coordinate axes x̂ (right), ŷ (into the page), ẑ (up).

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Find the force acting on the fluid due to the magnetic field (in terms of $L$, $B$, $h$, $w$, $\rho$ and the new velocity $v$) *[2.0 pts]*

answer.note: Official solution: the force is in the −x direction.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Derive an expression for the new speed $v$ of the fluid (in terms of $v_0$, $P$, $L$, $B$ and $\rho$ ) after the magnetic field is applied. *[3.0 pts]*

parts.label: c)
parts.statement: Derive an expression for the additional power that must be supplied by the turbine to increase the speed to its original value $v_0$. Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[2.0 pts]*

parts.label: d)
parts.statement: Now the magnetic field is turned off and mercury is replaced by water flowing with speed $v_0$. An electromagnetic wave with a single frequency is sent along the section with length $L$ in the direction of the flow. The refractive index of water is $n$, and $v_0\ll c$. Derive an expression for the contribution of the fluid’s motion to the phase difference between the waves entering and leaving section $L$. Copy your result onto the **answer form.** *[3.0 pts]*

sections.title: Part 3a
sections.statement:
The net force on a charged particle must be zero in the steady state

$$\vec F=0=q\vec E+q\vec v x\vec B$$

$$\vec E=-\vec v x\vec B=vB\,\hat{y}$$

(0.4 pts)

$$V_H=vBw$$

$$I=\frac{V_H}{R}=\frac{V_H}{\frac{\rho w}{Lh}}=\frac{vBwLh}{\rho w}=\frac{vBLh}{\rho}\ ,\ \text{direction: }-\hat{y}$$

(0.6 pts)

$$\vec F=I\vec\ell x\vec B=\frac{vB^2Lhw}{\rho}\ ,\ \text{direction: }(-\hat{y}\,x\,\hat{z}=-\hat{x})$$

Force is in the -x direction (0.8 pts)

This creates a back pressure $P_b$

$$P_b=\frac{vB^2Lhw}{\rho hw}=\frac{vB^2L}{\rho}$$

(0.6 pts)

$F_{net}=(P-P_b)hw$, (0.6 pts)

$v=\alpha F_{net}$ (0.4 pts)

$$v=\alpha(P-P_b)hw=\alpha\left(P-\frac{vB^2L}{\rho}\right)\frac{v_0}{\alpha P}=v_0-\frac{vv_0B^2L}{P\rho}$$

$$v\left(1+\frac{v_0B^2L}{P\rho}\right)=v_0$$

$$v=v_0\left(1+\frac{v_0B^2L}{P\rho}\right)^{-1}$$

$$v=v_0\frac{P\rho}{P\rho+v_0B^2L}$$

(0.6 pts)

figures.alt: Box-shaped pipe section of length L with pressure P applied at the left end (arrow), flow velocity v to the right, and three upward arrows B below the section; axes z (up), y (into the page) and x (right).

sections.title: Part 3b
sections.statement:
From conservation of energy:

$$\Delta Power=V_HI=\frac{v_0^2B^2whL}{\rho}$$

or,

to recover $v_0$ the pump must supply an additional pressure $\Delta P=P_b$ **(1.0 pts)**

$$\Delta Power=\Delta Phwv_0=P_bhwv_0=\frac{v_0^2B^2whL}{\rho}$$

sections.title: Part 3c
sections.statement:
1. $u=\dfrac{c}{n}$ $\qquad u'=\dfrac{\frac{c}{n}+v}{1+\frac{c}{n}\frac{v}{c^2}}=\dfrac{\frac{c}{n}+v}{1+\frac{v}{cn}}$ (0.5 pts)

   For small v ($v\ll c$);

   neglect the terms containing $\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$ in the expansion of $\left(1+\dfrac{v}{cn}\right)^{-1}$

   $$u'=\left(\frac{c}{n}+v\right)\frac{1}{1+\frac{v}{cn}}\approx\left(\frac{c}{n}+v\right)\left(1-\frac{v}{cn}\right)\approx\frac{c}{n}+v\left(1-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)$$

   $$\Delta u=u'-u\approx v\left(1-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)$$

   (0.5 pts)

   $$\Delta\phi=2\pi f\Delta T\ ,\ T=\frac{L}{u},\ \ \Delta\mathrm{T}=\frac{\Delta\mathrm{u}}{\mathrm{u}^2}L\approx\frac{Lv}{c^2}(n^2-1)$$

   (0.5 pts)

   $v=v_0$ so that, $\Delta\phi=2\pi f\dfrac{L}{c^2}(n^2-1)v_0$ (0.5 pts)

2. $\Delta\phi=2\pi f\dfrac{L}{c^2}(n^2-1)v_0$

   a phase of $\pi/36$ results in (0.4 pts)

   $$v_0=\frac{c^2}{72L(n^2-1)f}$$

   (0.2 pts)

   $$v_0=\frac{9x10^{16}}{72x10^{-1}x(2.56-1)x25}=3.2x10^{14}\ m/s$$

   which is not physical. (0.4 pts)

3. For v=20 m/s, $f\approx4\times10^{14}$ Hz. But for this value of f, skin depth is about 25 nm. This means that amplitude of the signal reaching the end of the tube is practically zero. Therefore mercury should be replaced with water. (0.6 pts)

   On the other hand if water is used instead of mercury, at 25 Hz $\delta\approx3\times10^{5}$ m. Signal reaches to the end but $v\approx6\times10^{14}$ m/s, is still nonphysical. Therefore frequency should be readjusted. (0.6 pts)

   For v=20 m/s electromagnetic wave of $f\approx8\times10^{14}$ Hz has a skin depth of about δ≈5.6 cm in water and the emerging wave is out of phase by $\pi/36$ with respect to the incident wave. (The amplitude of the wave reaching to the end of the section is about 17% of the incident amplitude). (0.6 pts)

   Therefore mercury should be replaced with water and frequency should be adjusted to $f\approx8\times10^{14}$ Hz. The correct choice is (iii) (0.2 pts)
